\chapter{Communication Complexity --- Transcript}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from TCSlib.CommunicationComplexity.DeterministicCC.Transcript
\section{Overview}

This module develops the theory of \emph{syntactic transcripts} for deterministic
two-party protocols.  A transcript records the complete Boolean message sequence
produced by a fixed execution path of a protocol; the module establishes that every
transcript's input set is a combinatorial rectangle, that executing the protocol on a
pair $(x,y)$ yields a unique transcript, and that the number of distinct transcripts is
at most $2^{\mathrm{complexity}(p)}$.  It also provides the swap and comap transport
operations on transcripts, both shown to be injective.

\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Syntactic transcript type]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.Transcript}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.Transcript}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol}
For a deterministic protocol $p$ over input types $X$ and $Y$ with output type $\alpha$,
the type $\mathrm{Transcript}(p)$ records the full message sequence of an execution path:
a terminal protocol has a single transcript (unit), while a communication node
contributes one Boolean bit together with the transcript of the chosen child protocol.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Output of a transcript]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.Transcript.output}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.Transcript.output}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.Transcript, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptSwap}
Given a syntactic transcript $t$ of a protocol $p$, \texttt{Transcript.output}~$t$ returns
the output value $\alpha$ attached to the leaf of the execution path described by $t$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Input set of a transcript]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.Transcript.inputSet}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.Transcript.inputSet}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.Transcript, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptSwap}
For a syntactic transcript $t$ of $p$, the \emph{input set} $\mathrm{inputSet}(t)
\subseteq X \times Y$ is the set of all input pairs $(x, y)$ whose execution of $p$
follows exactly the path described by $t$.  It is defined recursively: for a terminal
protocol it is $X \times Y$, and for a communication node it is the subset of pairs
where the current player's Boolean function matches the bit recorded in $t$ and the
remaining pair belongs to the child transcript's input set.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Input set is a rectangle]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.Transcript.inputSet_isRectangle}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.Transcript.inputSet_isRectangle}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.Transcript, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.Transcript.inputSet, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptSwap, CommunicationComplexity.Rectangle.IsRectangle}
\difficulty{5}
For every protocol $p$ and every syntactic transcript $t$ of $p$, the input set
$\mathrm{inputSet}(t)$ is a combinatorial rectangle, i.e.\ there exist sets $A \subseteq X$
and $B \subseteq Y$ such that $\mathrm{inputSet}(t) = A \times B$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Execute protocol to transcript]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcript}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcript}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.Transcript, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptSwap}
Given a protocol $p$ and an input pair $xy \in X \times Y$, \texttt{Protocol.transcript}~$p$~$xy$
executes $p$ on $xy$ and returns the syntactic transcript reached, recording each Boolean
message sent along the way.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Input follows its own transcript]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.mem_transcript}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.mem_transcript}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.Transcript.inputSet, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcript, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptSwap}
\difficulty{2}
For every protocol $p$ and every input pair $xy$, the pair $xy$ belongs to the input set
of its own computed transcript: $xy \in \mathrm{inputSet}(p.\mathrm{transcript}(xy))$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Transcript determined by membership]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcript_eq_of_mem}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcript_eq_of_mem}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.Transcript, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.Transcript.inputSet, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcript, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptSwap}
\difficulty{5}
If an input pair $xy$ belongs to the input set of a syntactic transcript $t$ of $p$,
then $t$ is exactly the transcript computed by running $p$ on $xy$:
$p.\mathrm{transcript}(xy) = t$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Protocol output equals transcript output]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.run_eq_transcript_output}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.run_eq_transcript_output}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.Transcript.output, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.run, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcript, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptSwap}
\difficulty{2}
For every protocol $p$ and input pair $xy$, running $p$ yields the same result as
reading the output from the computed transcript:
$p.\mathrm{run}(xy.1, xy.2) = \mathrm{Transcript.output}(p.\mathrm{transcript}(xy))$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Same transcript implies same output]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.run_eq_of_transcript_eq}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.run_eq_of_transcript_eq}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.Transcript.output, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.run, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.run_eq_transcript_output, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcript, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptSwap}
\difficulty{3}
If two input pairs $xy$ and $xy'$ produce the same syntactic transcript under $p$, then
they also produce the same protocol output:
$p.\mathrm{transcript}(xy) = p.\mathrm{transcript}(xy')$ implies
$p.\mathrm{run}(xy.1, xy.2) = p.\mathrm{run}(xy'.1, xy'.2)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Auxiliary bound on transcript count]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.card_transcript_le_two_pow_complexity_aux}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.card_transcript_le_two_pow_complexity_aux}
\leanok
\difficulty{4}
For natural numbers $a, b, c_a, c_b$ with $a \le 2^{c_a}$ and $b \le 2^{c_b}$, one has
$a + b \le 2^{1 + \max(c_a, c_b)}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Number of transcripts bounded by complexity]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.card_transcript_le_two_pow_complexity}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.card_transcript_le_two_pow_complexity}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.Transcript, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.card_transcript_le_two_pow_complexity_aux, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.complexity, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptSwap}
\difficulty{5}
A deterministic protocol $p$ has at most $2^{\mathrm{complexity}(p)}$ syntactic
transcripts: $|\mathrm{Transcript}(p)| \le 2^{p.\mathrm{complexity}}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Transcript swap]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptSwap}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptSwap}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.Transcript, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.swap}
Given a syntactic transcript $t$ of $p$, \texttt{transcriptSwap}~$t$ is the corresponding
transcript of the swapped protocol $p.\mathrm{swap}$ (where Alice and Bob exchange
roles), obtained by preserving the Boolean message sequence while reinterpreting each
node as the opposite player.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Transcript swap is injective]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptSwap_injective}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptSwap_injective}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptSwap}
\difficulty{6}
For every protocol $p$, the map \texttt{transcriptSwap} from $\mathrm{Transcript}(p)$ to
$\mathrm{Transcript}(p.\mathrm{swap})$ is injective: distinct transcripts of $p$ give
distinct transcripts of the swapped protocol.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Swap commutes with transcript computation]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptSwap_transcript}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptSwap_transcript}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.swap, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcript, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptSwap}
\difficulty{3}
For every protocol $p$ and inputs $x \in X$, $y \in Y$, swapping the transcript of $p$
on $(x, y)$ equals the transcript of the swapped protocol on the reversed pair $(y, x)$:
$\mathrm{transcriptSwap}(p.\mathrm{transcript}(x, y)) = p.\mathrm{swap}.\mathrm{transcript}(y, x)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Transcript comap]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptComap}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptComap}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.Transcript, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.comap, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptSwap}
Given maps $f_X : X' \to X$ and $f_Y : Y' \to Y$ and a syntactic transcript $t$ of
$p$, \texttt{transcriptComap}~$p$~$f_X$~$f_Y$~$t$ is the corresponding transcript of
the pulled-back protocol $p.\mathrm{comap}(f_X, f_Y)$, obtained by preserving the
Boolean message sequence while re-routing through the input maps.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Transcript comap is injective]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptComap_injective}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptComap_injective}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptComap, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptSwap}
\difficulty{6}
For every protocol $p$ and input maps $f_X : X' \to X$, $f_Y : Y' \to Y$, the map
\texttt{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptComap}~$p$~$f_X$~$f_Y$ from $\mathrm{Transcript}(p)$ to
$\mathrm{Transcript}(p.\mathrm{comap}(f_X, f_Y))$ is injective.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Comap commutes with transcript computation]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptComap_transcript}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptComap_transcript}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.comap, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcript, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptComap, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.transcriptSwap}
\difficulty{3}
For every protocol $p$, maps $f_X : X' \to X$, $f_Y : Y' \to Y$, and inputs
$x' \in X'$, $y' \in Y'$, pulling back the transcript of $p$ on $(f_X(x'), f_Y(y'))$
equals the transcript of the comapped protocol on $(x', y')$:
$\mathrm{transcriptComap}(p,f_X,f_Y,p.\mathrm{transcript}(f_X(x'),f_Y(y')))
= (p.\mathrm{comap}(f_X,f_Y)).\mathrm{transcript}(x',y')$.
\end{theorem}
